hints: Recall the rule given: compare the wavelength $\lambda$ of each wave with the size of its named obstruction.
Estimate orders of magnitude: microwaves are centimetres, radio waves are metres, sound in air is centimetres to metres, visible light is nanometres.
Estimate the obstructions: a post is centimetres, a wire and a hair are sub-millimetre, a gate post is about $0.1 \text{ m}$ - look for the closest match.
walkthrough: The question states maximum diffraction occurs when wavelength $\lambda$ is similar in size to the obstruction.

Estimate typical wavelengths in air: microwaves $\sim 10^{-2} \text{ m}$, radio waves $\sim 1 \text{ m}$ to $10^{2} \text{ m}$, audible sound $\sim 10^{-2} \text{ m}$ to $10^{1} \text{ m}$, visible light $\sim 5 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$.
Estimate obstruction sizes: steel post $\sim 10^{-2} \text{ m}$, copper wire $\sim 10^{-3} \text{ m}$, human hair $\sim 5 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}$, gate post $\sim 10^{-1} \text{ m}$.
Compare ratios: only microwaves and the steel post are both of order centimetres, so $\lambda$ divided by obstruction size is of order 1.
The other pairs are mismatched by factors of $10^{3}$ or more, giving very weak diffraction.
Therefore microwaves passing a steel post best demonstrates diffraction. This is option A

options.A: Microwave wavelength is of order centimetres, e.g. $\lambda \approx 0.03 \text{ m}$, and a steel post width is also of order centimetres, so $\lambda$ and obstruction match for strong diffraction.
options.B: Radio wavelength is of order metres to hundreds of metres, much larger than a millimetre-diameter copper wire, so sizes are not similar.
options.C: Audible sound wavelength is about $0.02 \text{ m}$ to $20 \text{ m}$, much larger than a human hair of width about $50 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$.
options.D: Visible light wavelength is about $500 \text{ nm}$, much smaller than a gate post of width about $0.1 \text{ m}$, so little diffraction occurs.
